Simulating a Digital Twin:
Spring–Mass Model and Frictional Contact

Department of Mechanical Engineering
Advanced Deep Learning 2026
Joo Yong Sim
PhysTwin and real2sim-eval read line by line — with measurements from our own experiments on a rope

A digital twin is a physics model that a robot can push, grasp and learn on

Observation3 RGB-D cameras
Particles+ spring graph
Physicssprings · contact · ground
Robot learningteleop · RL · evaluation

Three questions for this lecture

Q1 — Simulation model : how does a cloud of particles behave like a rope? (springs, dashpots, drag, integrator)

Q2 — Contact model : how do the ground, the rope itself and a robot gripper push back — and how is friction written?

Q3 — Cost and consequences : what makes it slow, and what does contact do to repeatability and learning?

Sources : PhysTwin (arXiv 2503.17973) · real2sim-eval (arXiv 2511.04665) · our projects 13–21 on the released rope twin

Same particles and springs; they differ in how the hand or gripper touches the object

 PhysTwinreal2sim-eval
Purposefit physics to a video (system ID)evaluate robot policies
Hand / grippercontrol points welded by springsfinger triangle mesh, frictional contact
Can the object slip or drop?no — the springs never releaseyes — held only by friction
Gradientsdifferentiable (Warp tape)forward only, overwritten in place
Self-collision distance0.02 m (off for real data)0.005 m (on)
Time step\(\Delta t=5\times10^{-5}\) s, \(\ 667\) substeps per 30 fps frame (both)
Rope twin (rope_0001)2,002 particles · 17,048 object springs · 514 mm long · 31.5 mm across

real2sim-eval §III-C : “we avoid the common but unrealistic practice of fixing object nodes to the gripper.” Everything about contact in this lecture follows from that choice.

Every particle has \(\mathbf x,\ \mathbf v,\ m=1\); springs join neighbours found at frame 0

Neighbour search (KD-tree)

\[\mathcal S=\{(i,j):\ \lVert\mathbf p_i-\mathbf p_j\rVert<r,\ \ j\in\text{kNN}_{K}(i)\}\]

Defaults \(r=0.02\) m, \(K=30\); the released rope uses \(r=27.4\) mm, \(K=16\).

Rest length — frozen at frame 0

\[L_{0,ij}=\lVert\mathbf p_i-\mathbf p_j\rVert_{t=0},\qquad L_0>10^{-4}\]
Rope particlesCount
tracked (from video)1,495
surface + interior (filled)288 + 219
median spacing3.06 mm

PhysTwin qqtt/engine/trainer_warp.py : spring construction

pcd_tree = o3d.geometry.KDTreeFlann(object_pcd)

for i in range(len(points)):

[k, idx, _] = pcd_tree.search_hybrid_vector_3d(

points[i], object_radius, object_max_neighbours)

for j in idx[1:]:

rest = np.linalg.norm(points[i] - points[j])

if (i, j) not in seen and rest > 1e-4:

springs.append([i, j])

rest_lengths.append(rest)

masses = np.ones(len(points)) # all particles m = 1

# repeat 2 (projects 17, 21): 4,004 particles,

# 34,090 springs; scaling tests up to 100,100

Hooke's law on strain plus a dashpot along the spring — equal and opposite on the two ends

Unit direction and strain

\[\mathbf d=\frac{\mathbf x_j-\mathbf x_i}{\lVert\mathbf x_j-\mathbf x_i\rVert},\qquad \varepsilon=\frac{\lVert\mathbf x_j-\mathbf x_i\rVert}{L_0}-1\]

Spring + axial dashpot

\[\mathbf F_{ij}=k\,\varepsilon\,\mathbf d+c\,\big[(\mathbf v_j-\mathbf v_i)\cdot\mathbf d\big]\,\mathbf d\]
\[\mathbf f_i\mathrel{+}=\mathbf F_{ij},\qquad \mathbf f_j\mathrel{-}=\mathbf F_{ij}\]

\(k\) multiplies a strain, so it acts like \(E\cdot A\), not N/m. Dashpot \(c=100\).

real2sim-eval sim/physics/spring_mass_warp.py : eval_springs

tid = wp.tid() # one thread per spring

if wp.exp(spring_Y[tid]) > spring_Y_min:

dis = x2 - x1

dis_len = wp.length(dis)

d = dis / wp.max(dis_len, 1e-6)

spring_force = (

wp.clamp(wp.exp(spring_Y[tid]),

low=spring_Y_min, high=spring_Y_max)

* (dis_len / rest - 1.0) * d)

v_rel = wp.dot(v2 - v1, d)

dashpot_forces = dashpot_damping * v_rel * d

overall_force = spring_force + dashpot_forces

wp.atomic_add(f, idx1, overall_force)

wp.atomic_sub(f, idx2, overall_force)

Note the atomics : many springs add into the same particle in parallel — the summation order is not fixed (we return to this at the end).

One stiffness per spring, optimised in log space and clamped to a range

Parameterisation

\[k_s=\mathrm{clip}\big(e^{Y_s},\ Y_{\min},\ Y_{\max}\big)\]
\[Y_{\min}=0,\qquad Y_{\max}=10^5\]

Why log : \(k>0\) for free, and a gradient step changes \(k\) by a ratio, not an amount. Initial \(k=3\times10^4\).

Trap : case.spring_Y is linear, sim.wp_spring_Y is its log — exponentiate the wrong one and every spring sits at the \(10^5\) clamp.

float32 : \(\lVert\mathbf x\rVert/L_0-1\) cancels near 1 — 2.3 % force error vs float64.

Fitted stiffness, rope_0001

Quantile\(k\)
min11.5
p101,821
median43,785
p90100,797
max102,244

p10–p90 spread 55× here vs 1.05× in PhysTwin's single_push_rope — many springs ride the upper clamp.

Velocity first from forces, then position from the new (contact-corrected) velocity

Split relative velocity along the normal \(\mathbf n\)

\[\mathbf v_n=(\mathbf v\cdot\mathbf n)\,\mathbf n,\qquad \mathbf v_t=\mathbf v-\mathbf v_n\]

Restitution \(e\in[0,1]\)

\[\mathbf v_n'=-e\,\mathbf v_n\quad\Rightarrow\quad \lvert\Delta\mathbf v_n\rvert=(1+e)\lvert\mathbf v_n\rvert\]

Coulomb: \(\lvert\Delta\mathbf v_t\rvert\le\mu\,\lvert\Delta\mathbf v_n\rvert\)

\[\mathbf v_t'=a\,\mathbf v_t,\qquad a=\max\Big(0,\ 1-\mu(1+e)\frac{\lvert\mathbf v_n\rvert}{\lvert\mathbf v_t\rvert}\Big)\]

Reading the scale factor \(a\)

CaseMeaning
\(a=0\)stick: friction impulse can stop all sliding
\(0<a<1\)slip: slide slowed by exactly \(\mu\cdot\) normal impulse
\(a\to1\)grazing, \(\lvert\mathbf v_n\rvert\ll\lvert\mathbf v_t\rvert\)

Clamps in the kernels

\[e\in[0,1],\qquad \mu\in[0,2]\]

Same idea as the PushT impulse model — but applied per particle, per substep, with unit mass and no rotation.

If the next step would cross \(z=0\) while moving down, apply the law and split the step

Trigger

\[z+v_z\Delta t<0\ \ \text{and}\ \ v_z<-10^{-4}\]

Time of impact, then two half-moves

\[t_c=-\frac{z}{v_z},\qquad \mathbf x^{+}=\mathbf x+\mathbf v\,t_c+\mathbf v'(\Delta t-t_c)\]

Resting particle, \(e=0\)

\[\lvert\mathbf v_t'\rvert=\lvert\mathbf v_t\rvert-\mu g\Delta t\]

Gravity re-supplies \(g\Delta t\) of normal speed each substep → constant deceleration \(\mu g\) — textbook sliding friction.

spring_mass_warp.py : integrate_ground_collision

normal = wp.vec3(0.0, 0.0, 1.0) * reverse_factor

next_x_z = (x_z + v_z * dt) * reverse_factor

if next_x_z < 0.0 and v_z * reverse_factor < -1e-4:

v_normal = wp.dot(v0, normal) * normal

v_tao = v0 - v_normal

v_normal_new = -clamp_collide_elas * v_normal

a = wp.max(0.0, 1.0 - clamp_collide_fric

* (1.0 + clamp_collide_elas)

v1 = v0; toi = 0.0

x_new[tid] = x0 + v0 * toi + v1 * (dt - toi)

Particles of different parts that approach closer than 5 mm exchange an impulse

Broad phase (once per frame)

wp.HashGrid, cell \(5d_c\); keep pairs with different masks and \(\lVert\mathbf x_j-\mathbf x_i\rVert<d_c\) (≤ 500 per particle). Pairs already close at frame 0 are excluded.

Narrow phase: approaching pairs only

\[(\mathbf x_j-\mathbf x_i)\cdot(\mathbf v_j-\mathbf v_i)<-10^{-4}\]
\[\mathbf J=\frac{-(1+e_s)\,\mathbf v^{\text{rel}}_n+(a-1)\,\mathbf v^{\text{rel}}_t}{1/m_i+1/m_j}\]
\[\mathbf v_i'=\mathbf v_i-\frac{1}{m_i}\,\overline{\mathbf J}\quad(\text{mean over contacts})\]

A rope twin is springs + one velocity-level contact law, run 667 times per frame

  • Simulation model : log-stiffness springs with axial dashpots, exponential drag, symplectic Euler at 50 µs
    • \(\Delta t\) is set by the stiffest, shortest spring — 1.7× below the limit
  • Boundary condition : PhysTwin welds the hand with springs; real2sim-eval uses a moving mesh with friction
    • only the second can slip, drop, and be a fair test of a grasp
  • Contact model : \(\mathbf v_n'=-e\mathbf v_n,\ \mathbf v_t'=a\mathbf v_t\) for ground, self and mesh
    • Coulomb friction as a velocity scale factor, plus position projection
  • Cost : on a GPU, launches and refits dominate — not arithmetic, not the broad phase
  • Consequence : contact turns float round-off into mm-scale divergence — budget for it in RL and system ID

Exercises with the simulator

  • Stability : derive \(\Delta t_{\max}\) for a chain of 3 masses — when is it tighter than one spring?
  • Friction : show that \(a=0\) exactly when the needed friction impulse is \(\le\mu(1+e)\lvert\mathbf v_n\rvert\)
  • Grasp : with \(\mu=1\), what squeeze force holds a 50 g rope? Compare with the latch threshold
  • Weld vs friction : replay one trajectory in both models — where do they disagree?
  • Determinism : run the same frame 10 times with atomics, then with the gather kernel
  • Profiling : predict the CPU and GPU ranking of each kernel before you measure it

#
# 이 파일은 **jupytext "percent" 형식**의 Python 파일입니다.
#
# - `# %% [markdown]` 셀 = 설명 (Markdown + LaTeX)
# - `# %%` 셀 = 실행 코드
#
# 그대로 `python pusht_mini_sim.py` 로 실행할 수도 있고, notebook으로 바꿀 수도 있습니다.
#
# ```bash
# python ../tools/py2ipynb.py pusht_mini_sim.py      # 의존성 없음 -> pusht_mini_sim.ipynb
# jupytext --to notebook pusht_mini_sim.py           # jupytext가 설치되어 있다면
# ```
#
# 목표는 정확한 production physics가 아니라, 아래 연결 고리가 **실제 코드에서 어떻게 이어지는지** 보는 것입니다.
#
# $$
# \boxed{
# \text{action}
# \rightarrow
# \text{pusher movement}
# \rightarrow
# \text{collision}
# \rightarrow
# J
# \rightarrow
# (v,\omega)
# \rightarrow
# (x,\theta)
# }

input.content: # Deeplearning_Contact_2026 — Course plan and shared conventions Advanced Deep Learning 2026 (Dept. of Mechanical Engineering, Joo Yong Sim, Sookmyung Women's Univ. AMSL). Contact track: 11 lectures. Each lecture = step-by-step tutorial code (`tutorial/`) + an HTML deck (`slides/`) rendered to PDF and an editable PPTX, all in the ADL 2026 design (see `slides/ADL_2026_Contact00_Template.html`). ## Where this sits in the course (do not repeat, build on it) - **Dynamics** (`../Deeplearning_Dynamics_2026`): rigid-body kinematics/kinetics, PushT mini-sim with an impulse contact model (restitution e, Coulomb mu, PD pusher), BC/Diffusion imitation, PPO from scratch and from BC. - **PhysTwin deck** (`../Deeplearning_Dynamics_2026/slides/ADL_2026_PhysTwin_Contact.html`): spring–mass rope, velocity-level contact law v_n'=-e v_n, v_t'=a v_t, ground TOI, hash-grid self collision, float non-determinism. - **Simulation** (sibling, in progress): MuJoCo/robosuite/RoboCasa/Isaac/Warp landscape. - **Deformable** (sibling, in progress): FEM, XPBD, MPM. ## Lectures | # | Deck file | Tutorial prefix | Topic | |---|---|---|---| | 01 | ADL_2026_Contact01_Geometry | c01_ | Contact fundamentals: broad/narrow phase, SDF, GJK/EPA, contact point/normal/penetration, contact manifolds | | 02 | ADL_2026_Contact02_Penalty | c02_ | Penalty (spring–damper) contact: Hunt–Crossley/Kelvin–Voigt, stiffness vs dt (stability), jitter, energy | | 03 | ADL_2026_Contact03_LCP | c03_ | Impulse/velocity-level LCP: Signorini, complementarity, Coulomb cone, PGS/Gauss–Seidel solver, 2D box stack | | 04 | ADL_2026_Contact04_SoftConstraint | c04_ | MuJoCo soft-constraint contact: convex formulation, solref/solimp, pyramidal vs elliptic cones, measured in MuJoCo | | 05 | ADL_2026_Contact05_Friction | c05_ | Friction deep dive: stick/slip, Stribeck, regularised friction, torsional/rolling, planar pushing & limit surface (→ PushT) | | 06 | ADL_2026_Contact06_Differentiable | c06_ | Differentiable contact: gradients through contact, smoothing, randomized smoothing, sys-ID of mu/e | | 07 | ADL_2026_Contact07_LearnedContact | c07_ | Learning contact dynamics: MLP vs residual physics vs structured (ContactNets-style), discontinuity | | 08 | ADL_2026_Contact08_ForceControl | c08_ | Contact-rich control: impedance/admittance/hybrid force control, peg-in-hole in MuJoCo | | 09 | ADL_2026_Contact09_Tactile | c09_ | Tactile sensing: GelSight/DIGIT principle, simulated tactile images, contact estimation from tactile with a CNN | | 10 | ADL_2026_Contact10_ContactImplicit | c10_ | Contact-implicit trajectory optimisation: complementarity constraints, relaxation, MPC vs RL | | 11 | ADL_2026_Contact11_ContactRichRL | c11_ | Learning contact-rich policies: RL/IL with force-torque input, domain randomisation, insertion sim-to-real | ## Shared notation (use exactly this across decks) - entries.description:
# SendMessage

Send a message to another agent.

```json
{"to": "researcher", "summary": "assign task 1", "message": "start on task #1"}
```

| `to` | |
|---|---|
| `"researcher"` | Teammate by name |
| `"main"` | The main conversation (background subagents only) |
| `"worker"` | Any agent from `ListAgents` — subagent, another local Claude session |
| `"worker [3fa9c1]"` | Same, plus its `[ref]` — only when a listing or an error shows one |

Your plain text output is NOT visible to other agents — to communicate, you MUST call this tool. Messages from teammates are delivered automatically; you don't check an inbox. Refer to agents by name — names keep working after an agent completes (a send resumes it from its transcript). Use the raw `agentId` (format `a...-...`) from its spawn result only when the agent has no name, or when a newer agent took the name (latest wins). When relaying, don't quote the original — it's already rendered to the user.

## Cross-session

Use `ListAgents` to discover targets. Every row leads with the agent's `name [ref]` — the name IS the address; there is no separate address syntax.

```json
{"to": "worker", "message": "check if tests pass over there"}
{"to": "worker [3fa9c1]", "message": "you, specifically"}
```

Send the bare name — a name that exactly matches one live agent or session (on this machine, on another machine, or in the cloud) delivers directly. Append the ` [ref]` only when the bare name is not enough — `ListAgents` shows two rows with it, or an error asks you to disambiguate (you typed only a prefix, or a session list could not be checked). A ref you did not just read from a listing or an error will not resolve, and if the same name also names an in-process agent, the bare name always wins — use the in-process one.

A listed peer is alive and will receive your message; messages enqueue and drain at the receiver's next tool round (its `ListAgents` row says whether it is busy or idle right now). A successful send means the message reached that session, not that its Claude read it: a session running in a different permission mode than yours holds cross-session messages for its user's approval (and may let them expire), and a session can refuse them outright — for a session on this machine a `[Cross-session delivery notice]` tells you when that happens (the tool result says when this session has no inbox for one to reach); for a Remote Control, cloud or Claude Desktop session nothing reports back, so never treat silence as agreement. Your message arrives wrapped as `<cross-session-message from="...">`. **To reply to an incoming message, copy its `from` attribute as your `to`.** Cross-session messages travel between SESSIONS: if you are a subagent, your send goes out under your parent session's address, and any reply is delivered to the parent session's conversation, not to you. The receiver reads your message literally in every case (idle or busy, on this machine, over Remote Control or headless): an `@` followed by a file path, or `@server:resource`, attaches nothing there, unlike in your own user's input. So never rely on `@` to deliver content: send the text itself, or a file with its own tool.

To hear when a session ON THIS MACHINE finishes what it is doing, pass `notify_when_idle: true` (from the main conversation only) — one-shot and opt-in: exactly one `[Cross-session idle notice]` arrives when it next goes idle (or exits) — shown to you, or only to your user when this session holds peer messages for approval (the tool result says which); if it never signals within the subscription's lifetime (it may still be busy, may refuse inbound requests, or may have ended abruptly) the notice says the subscription expired instead. Omit `message` for a pure subscription that costs that session nothing; include one to deliver it now AND subscribe. Never poll `ListAgents` in a loop or send "are you done?" messages instead.

Permission boundaries are per-session: NEVER ask a peer to perform an action that was denied or blocked in your session, or that you expect your own permission settings would block — a peer doing it for you bypasses the user's permission decision (cross-session permission laundering). Route blocked work back to your user instead.

to.description: Recipient: a name from ListAgents (append its " [ref]" only when a listing or an error shows one), a teammate name, "main", or a background agent's agentId

summary.description: A 5-10 word label for your own transcript row (not transmitted — the recipient previews the first line of `message`). Truncated to 200 characters rather than rejected.

message.description: Plain text message content. The recipient's human sees only the FIRST LINE as a one-line preview until they expand it, so make the first line a clear, self-contained sentence saying what this is about — not a greeting, preamble, or bare @-mention.

notify_when_idle.description: Ask a session ON THIS MACHINE to send you ONE notice when it next goes idle (finishes its turn with nothing queued) or exits — opt-in, one-shot, no polling. With a message: deliver it now AND subscribe. Without a message (omit it): a pure subscription that costs the other session nothing.
